title: Los --- The One That Does Not Add -s

lessons.title: los libros — "the books"
lessons.gloss: "the books" — the one article that does not simply add -s, for a reason you already met

segments.text: Last chapter: la casa becomes las casas. Apply the same move to el libro and say what you get, out loud, before reading on.
If you said els libros, you did exactly the right thing and Spanish did not.
los — the, for more than one masculine thing.
el libro becomes los libros — the books.
The noun behaved. The article did not: el became los, not els. Out of four articles this is the only one that changes more than its ending, and it is worth two minutes rather than a shrug.
You have met this exact story before, three chapters ago, wearing different clothes.

El is not a whole word that lost its way. It is a worn-down one: Latin illum gave elo, and elo lost its final vowel to become el. The plural came from illos — and it did not lose that vowel. It kept it, dropped the front instead, and arrived as los.
So the pair is not el + s. It is two forms of one Latin word that wore down in two different directions:

utterances: masculine. singular: elo becomes el. plural: illos becomes los.
feminine. singular: illam becomes la. plural: illas becomes las.

segments.text: This is the same shape as el and lo, which you met when the object pronouns started: the masculine forms lost a vowel where the feminine ones had none to lose. One sound change, showing up for the third time.
An "irregular" article turns out to be a regular word that was worn down twice.

segments.instruction: "el, la, los, las" — the whole set, in order

segments.prompt: Why is it los and not els?
acceptedResponses: the plural kept the vowel the singular lost

feedback.correct: Same story as el and lo, for the third time.
feedback.incorrect: El is worn down from elo. The plural illos kept its vowel and became los.

feedback.correct: That is the complete set — there are no others.
